items.title: [rabble.ca] Canadians rally nationwide against bill expanding fast-track project powers
items.content_html:
🏔️ ✏️

More than 65 protests took place across Canada on Nov. 12 against Bill C-39, the federal Building Canada Strong Act, which would let Cabinet designate regions of “national interest” and accelerate approvals for major projects. The bill could cover pipelines, energy infrastructure and industrial developments and would set a one-year timeline for decisions on designated projects. Indigenous, environmental and labour groups argue the bill could weaken environmental safeguards, treaty rights and workers’ ability to strike; the federal government says it would speed up projects supporting economic growth and energy security while maintaining Indigenous consultation. A House of Commons committee is studying the bill, and a special Senate committee is conducting a pre-study; no date for its final House vote has been publicly announced.

items.title: [nacion.com] Latin American countries raise the alarm over rising diabetes rates and underdiagnosis
items.content_html:
🏔️ ✏️

Health figures released for World Diabetes Day show diagnoses and undetected cases in several Latin American countries. Costa Rica reported 17,276 diagnoses in 2025, 28.62% more than in 2024; in Panama, the Social Security Fund treated around 53,000 people during 2025, while an estimated 312,800 adults were living with diabetes in 2024. In Mexico, more than 14 million adults have the disease, and nearly one in three is unaware of their diagnosis. National estimates do not necessarily use the same methods. In Brazil, an estimated five million people remain undiagnosed, in addition to the 16 million who have been diagnosed. In Argentina, nearly four in 10 people with abnormal test results were unaware of their condition. The International Diabetes Federation estimates that more than 589 million adults worldwide are living with diabetes. Type 2 diabetes can progress for years without clear symptoms; when blood glucose remains high, it can cause cardiovascular, kidney, vision, and nerve damage. Authorities and specialists recommend screening tests, clinical follow-up, and sustained lifestyle changes. Costa Rica recorded another 16,758 new cases up to the epidemiological week of October 18–24, 2026.

This weekend could mean misery for thousands of travellers in the United States as some flights across the country are delayed following yesterday’s (Nov. 13) nationwide grounding of all planes, including 3,600 cancellations. ​Delta Airlines has cancelled 20 per cent of its flights for Nov. 14, while United Airlines has cancelled 17 per cent and American Airlines has cancelled 15 per cent. ​The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) called for a full ground stop due to telecommunications outages, creating a serious backlog Saturday morning; however, some domestic flights have resumed. ​A post by the FAA adds that it has accounted for every flight and will handle international flights on a case-by-case basis. ​Secretary Sean Duffy provided an update on the FAA National Ground Stop last night, and is expected to be updating the public again on Saturday at 7:30 a.m. Pacific. ​“What we have is an incredibly old air traffic control system. Our switches, our routers actually got overloaded with data; they started giving us inconsistency in the data … and because of that we shut the system down.” ​The ground stop did not come from a threat to the United States and was not linked to this week’s Microsoft outage, according to Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullen. ​Travel impacts could last several days while airports and airlines comb through thousands of cancellations and delays.

items.title: [straitstimes.com] Leo XIV warns of rural exodus at Mass in the Peruvian Andes
items.content_html:
🏔️ ✏️

Pope Leo XIV warned on Saturday during a Mass in Santa Cruz de Succhabamba, in the Peruvian Andes, that poverty, forced migration, and the unequal distribution of resources are emptying rural communities. Around 20,000 people attended, according to the Vatican. Leo XIV, who led the Diocese of Chiclayo, thus fulfilled his promise to return to Peru, made before leaving for Rome in 2023. In his homily, he spoke of those who leave their towns to seek a better future in coastal cities and urged people to confront injustice without violence. Cajamarca, the region where Santa Cruz is located, has poverty rates of up to 40%, according to official figures cited by Reuters. On Saturday, Leo XIV also crowned the image of the Immaculate Conception at Chiclayo Cathedral and closed the jubilee year in Zaña, marking the 300th anniversary of the canonization of Saint Toribio de Mogrovejo. This Sunday, November 15, he travels to Cusco and Pucallpa, where he will meet with missionaries and representatives of Amazonian peoples; on Monday, November 16, he will celebrate the concluding Mass in Lima before departing for Rome.

items.title: [prensalibre.com] Guatemala imposes 30-day state of siege in Zacapa and Izabal
items.content_html:
🏔️ ✏️

Guatemalan President Bernardo Arévalo decreed a 30-day state of siege on November 14 in the eastern departments of Zacapa and Izabal, following a series of armed attacks that left seven people dead on Friday. The decree restricts movement and public gatherings, and allows security forces to detain suspects and search homes without a prior court order . The Army reported that it deployed between 400 and 600 soldiers to the area. The forces are conducting road checkpoints, patrols, and aerial reconnaissance in Zacapa, Izabal, and the neighboring department of Chiquimula. items.title: [theguardian.com] UN warns climate adaptation funding leaves vulnerable countries exposed
items.content_html:
🏔️ ✏️

A United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP) report says developing countries remain exposed to worsening floods, droughts and heat because adaptation funding is not reaching vulnerable communities at the scale required. Least-developed countries and small island states need an estimated $40 billion to $50 billion annually, equivalent to 3% to 4% of their gross domestic product, while support to least-developed countries fell 16% from 2022 to 2024. Adaptation measures include flood barriers, heat-resistant hospitals and drought-resilient water and farming systems. Low- and middle-income countries accounted for 99% of the 765 million people affected by floods and landslides between 2020 and 2025. Communities also face obstacles to turning plans into projects, including weak institutional coordination and difficulty accessing funding for climate-related losses. At the COP31 climate conference, opening in Antalya on Nov. 9, campaigners are urging governments to set out a concrete funding plan and prioritize grants or concessional loans over high-interest borrowing for projects that generate little direct revenue. Concessional loans are easier to repay than high-interest loans.

items.title: [corriere.it] Italy drops school staffing cuts, weighs wider 2027 budget changes
items.content_html:
🏔️ ✏️

The Italian government says it will remove a planned school staffing reduction from its 2027 budget and is considering further changes to health funding, pensions and tax measures as Parliament prepares amendments. The proposal would have reduced teaching and administrative posts by nearly 7,000; Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni said no existing employees would lose their jobs and described the measure as aligning future hiring with falling enrollment. Whether the staffing reduction will be cancelled outright or postponed until 2029 remains under discussion. Lawmakers have until 6 p.m. on Nov. 17 to submit amendments. Economy Minister Giancarlo Giorgetti is considering about €500 million in additional health funding, while the government is also weighing changes to the Superbonus tax-credit repayment rules and the proposed exit tax. A broader reversal of pension changes appears less likely, and all amendments must preserve the budget’s financial balances.

items.content_html:

Researchers believe low testosterone could be an important early warning sign of future health risks, particularly when levels fall below 8.6 nmol/L.

items.title: [proplanta.de] EU convenes crisis talks as freezer hacks spread to Germany, Romania
items.content_html:
🏔️ ✏️

The European Commission convened two crisis meetings after cyberattacks on supermarket refrigeration systems spread across Europe, with incidents reported in at least 11 countries, including Germany and Romania. The attacks remotely raised temperatures or triggered defrost cycles, forcing retailers to discard food; no group has claimed responsibility, and authorities have not established whether the incidents share a perpetrator. The wave follows a similar attack on French supermarkets in October. A store in Lilienthal, Germany, said it had to discard goods worth more than €360,000, while six Romanian stores were affected. Italy’s government held talks with intelligence and cybersecurity officials and said the impact there was limited to a small number of commercial sites; it reported no health risk from thawed food. EU officials are coordinating with national authorities, who are conducting the investigations. Agriculture Commissioner Christophe Hansen said the bloc’s food supply was not currently threatened, and the Commission said the incidents showed a need for stronger cybersecurity across the EU.

items.content_html:

Singapore Airlines said about 46,000 booking records may have been accessed in a breach at travel technology provider Amadeus, potentially exposing passenger names, booking references, itineraries and booking classes. items.title: [carbonbrief.org] El Niño-linked fires lift total carbon emissions despite fossil fuel dip
items.content_html:
🏔️ ✏️

El Niño-related peat fires and forest degradation in Southeast Asia are projected to push land-use carbon emissions higher in 2026, bringing total global CO₂ emissions to 43.3 billion tonnes even as fossil-fuel emissions edge down, according to the Global Carbon Project’s annual assessment. The researchers link the rise in land-use emissions to drier conditions and fires often ignited by human activity. The 21st Global Carbon Budget, published Nov. 10 in Earth System Science Data and presented during the U.N. climate conference in Antalya, projects 5.1 billion tonnes of emissions from land-use change this year. The projected decline in fossil-fuel emissions is partly attributable to the Iran conflict’s energy shock, alongside the growing contribution of solar, wind and electric vehicles. The report says the land carbon sink recovered in 2025 after weakening during the 2023-24 El Niño, but the strong 2026 El Niño is expected to weaken it again in 2027. Separately, an analysis of Chinese data found that emissions fell 3.1% in July-September, the country’s steepest quarterly drop since pandemic lockdowns in 2022.

items.title: [straitstimes.com] Prince Harry and five others seek permission to appeal in Daily Mail privacy case
items.content_html:
🏔️ ✏️

Prince Harry, the Duke of Sussex, and five other public figures have applied for permission to appeal the dismissal of their privacy claims against Associated Newspapers, publisher of the Daily Mail and Mail on Sunday. Their application, filed on Friday, Nov. 6, challenges both the High Court’s rejection of the claims and a later order on the publisher’s legal costs. The claimants alleged that journalists or people working for the publisher used unlawful information-gathering methods, including voicemail interception and deception; Associated Newspapers denied the allegations. After an 11-week trial, High Court judge Matthew Nicklin ruled on July 7 that none of the seven claimants had proved unlawful information gathering. He accepted journalists’ explanations that the articles came from lawful sources and said suspicion alone could not establish the claims. The claimants say the rulings are “legally and factually flawed”. In August, Nicklin ordered an initial payment of £9,544,355 toward the publisher’s costs, with the final amount to be determined at a separate hearing. He ordered costs to be assessed on an indemnity basis, which can allow greater recovery. Associated Newspapers estimated its defence costs at about £34.5 million by July 9. The Court of Appeal must first decide whether to grant permission to appeal.

items.title: [elpais.com] Cyberattacks on refrigeration systems fuel concerns about connected household appliances
items.content_html:
🏔️ ✏️

Cyberattacks on internet-connected refrigeration systems in supermarkets and French blood banks have destroyed food in Europe and heightened concerns about connected devices. Nearly 800 freezers were sabotaged in France and Northern Europe this week. On November 2, temperatures also rose in the cold rooms of a blood donation service in France. There, alarms and swift action prevented damage to stored blood. The targeted systems used internet-accessible controls for maintenance and remote operation. According to experts, similar attacks on private smart-home devices are less likely because, with typical router configurations, the devices cannot be accessed directly from the internet. Risks include outdated software, weak passwords, and devices with cameras or microphones. Germany’s Federal Office for Information Security recommends automatic updates, separate networks for smart-home devices, and unique passwords. The identity of those behind the attacks remains unclear.

items.title: [stpetersburg.usf.edu] Study finds drought could cut cactus habitat by 80% by 2100
items.content_html:
🏔️ ✏️

An international research team analyzed nearly 1,000 cactus species and found that more than a quarter could lose at least 80% of their suitable habitat by 2100 if severe droughts intensify. The researchers added drought projections to climate models, which commonly use long-term temperature and rainfall averages, and combined them with biodiversity records, field observations and community-science data. The projected losses could qualify affected species as Critically Endangered under criteria set by the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN), more than doubling the number of cacti in that category. Researchers say drought may also reduce growth or flowering without immediately killing plants, compounding threats from habitat destruction and illegal collection. The findings are expected to inform updated IUCN Red List assessments; the team says further research is needed to determine which life stages and biological processes drought affects.

items.title: [elpais.com] Leo XIV denounces racism against Afro-Peruvians and recalls slavery
items.content_html:
🏔️ ✏️

Pope Leo XIV denounced the discrimination that Afro-Peruvians continue to face on November 14 and recalled the slavery and humiliation suffered by their ancestors. He did so during a meeting in Zaña, a town in northern Peru recognized as a site commemorating slavery and African cultural heritage. Leo expressed his affection for the community and spoke about crime, extortion, and insecurity affecting families in the area. The pontiff, who was bishop of the Diocese of Chiclayo from 2015 to 2023, closed in Zaña the Jubilee Year marking the 300th anniversary of the canonization of Saint Toribio de Mogrovejo. In May, in his first encyclical, he had apologized on behalf of the Church for the role previous pontiffs played in legitimizing slavery in the Americas and for failing to condemn it for centuries. At the meeting, Analí Montenegro Mendoza, representative of the Afro-Peruvian community in the diocese, called for a Church in which no one feels inferior because of their skin color, history, or culture. Peru is the final stop on Leo's South American tour, which includes Argentina and Uruguay; he is expected to remain in the country until Monday, November 16.
